    "worldLore": {
      "Taverns and Inns": {
        "text": "Taverns and inns are where travellers eat, drink, sleep and hear the news. They come in four grades, and the name over the door usually tells which. The lowest are flophouses, doss-houses and dives (names like the Rat, the Bilge, the Gutter or the Hovel): straw pallets, thin stew and cheap drink. Most are common taverns and inns: plain rooms, honest food, a busy common room. Fine houses, lodges, manors, halls and garden inns offer clean private rooms and better cooking. The grand houses (Golden, Gilded, Silver, Royal, Crown, Jade, Palace and the like) serve nobles and rich merchants, and charge accordingly. The better the house, the higher every price, from a mug of ale to a bed.\n\nThe custom is the same everywhere: coin first. A room is paid in full before the key changes hands, for as many nights as the guest wants, up to two weeks at a time. Meals are included with a room; drink usually is not. A guest without a room pays for food and drink when it is served. Buying a round means paying for drinks for the whole table, about four. Keepers do not give credit, and anyone who tries to go up to a room without paying is stopped at the stairs.\n\nA paid room is the guest's until mid-morning (around the tenth hour) after the last paid night; after that the keeper wants the room back or another night's coin. A guest may haggle once over a quoted price. A good argument can bring it down by up to a quarter, a poor one leaves it where it was, and an insulting one can make the keeper raise it. After that the price is final."
      },
      "Gambling Houses and House Rules": {
        "text": "Card and dice games are played in most taverns and inns, and in gambling dens, card rooms and gaming houses, which keep the same rules as a common tavern. Three games are found almost everywhere: blackjack, higher or lower, and dice.\n\nEvery table has limits, set by the grade of the house: a dive takes only a few coins a bet, while a grand house takes large stakes. A stake outside the limits is simply refused. The stake is put down before the cards are dealt or the dice are thrown, and the house pays winners at once.\n\nThe house protects itself. A player who wins too much in one night (the limit is higher in better houses) is politely, then firmly, refused any more bets until the next day. Cheating, such as marked cards, palming, peeking, loaded dice or a trick throw, can be tried once a game. Done very well, it tips the game in the player's favour. Done badly, it gets the cheat caught: the stake is forfeit, they are barred from gambling there for the rest of the night, and the room deals with them as it sees fit. A player who walks away from a game in the middle is settled up fairly: a blackjack hand stands as it is, and a higher-or-lower pot is paid out."
      },
      "Blackjack": {
        "text": "Blackjack, also called twenty-one, is played against the dealer with a single deck. Number cards count their value, jacks, queens and kings count ten, and an ace counts eleven or one, whichever is better. The player and the dealer each get two cards; one of the dealer's is shown and the other is face down.\n\nAn ace with a ten-value card on the first two cards is a natural blackjack. It pays back the stake plus one and a half times it, unless the dealer also has one, in which case the stake is returned. If only the dealer has a natural, the player loses.\n\nOtherwise the player may hit (take another card), stand (keep the hand), double down (on the first two cards only: double the stake, take exactly one more card, then stand) or surrender (on the first two cards only: give up the hand and get half the stake back). Going over twenty-one is a bust and loses at once. When the player stands, the dealer draws until reaching seventeen or more. A dealer who busts loses. Otherwise the higher total wins: a win pays back twice the stake, a tie returns the stake, and a lower total loses it."
      },
      "Higher or Lower": {
        "text": "Higher or lower is a quick game of nerve played with one deck. Aces are high and twos are low. The player puts down a stake and the dealer turns a card. The player calls whether the next card will be higher or lower. A card of the same value counts as wrong. Calling higher on an ace, or lower on a two, is not allowed.\n\nEach right call grows the pot. A long-shot call grows it a lot, while a safe call grows it only a little, and the house always keeps a small cut. After each right call the player can cash out and take the whole pot, or risk it all on another call. One wrong call loses everything. The dealer pays out automatically after five right calls in a row, and no pot can grow past what the house is willing to lose in a night."
      },
      "Dice (High Throw)": {
        "text": "The simplest tavern game. The player and the house each throw two six-sided dice. The higher total wins: a win pays back twice the stake, a tie returns the stake, and a lower throw loses it. One throw settles each bet, which makes it the favourite game of drunks, sailors and anyone in a hurry."

      "barren-planet": {
        "text": "Barren planets are one of the most common planet types in the universe. They either are large enough to still retain a molten core and a thin atmosphere, or are too small and, without the magnetic field generated by a molten core, have had their atmosphere stripped away by solar radiation over geological time.\n\nTheir surfaces are constellated with meteorite craters of all sizes — from tiny pits barely visible on the rock to vast impact basins stretching hundreds of kilometers across. Deep cracks and fault lines crisscross the terrain, caused by the shrinking of the crust as it cooled and contracted over millions of years. These fissures can run for dozens of kilometers and sometimes expose layers of mineral deposits that would otherwise remain buried. The terrain is dominated by endless stretches of rock formations: jagged ridges, eroded mesas, dry valleys, and wind-sculpted stone shapes where any atmosphere remains.\n\nThey are warm enough not to be frozen worlds, but there is nothing but rock and dust there. No oceans, no rivers, no vegetation. The landscape is painted in shades of grey, brown, ochre, and rust, broken only by the occasional glint of a mineral vein or the dark shadow of a crater. Where the atmosphere has survived it is thin and barely breathable — often laden with fine dust that scatters the sunlight into pale, muted sunsets.\n\nDespite their desolation, barren planets are frequently targeted for mining operations. The exposed crust and impact-excavated basins make subsurface mineral veins relatively accessible, and the lack of biosphere means extraction can proceed without ecological concerns. Remote mining outposts, automated refineries, and company-run extraction colonies dot the more mineral-rich barren worlds.\n\nIn extremely rare cases, ruins can be found on the surface. These may be the remnants of previous mining operations abandoned when the veins ran dry or the economics shifted, or — far more rarely — the fossilized remains of an ancient civilization that once thrived on a living world before a cataclysm stripped it of everything: atmosphere, water, and life, leaving only stone where cities once stood. Such ruins are prized by archaeologists, scavengers, and treasure hunters alike, though most barren worlds hold nothing but rock and silence."

      "cryo-volcanic-planet": {
        "text": "Cryovolcanic planets are a subclass of frozen worlds where the core remains hot enough to periodically cause eruptions, but not hot enough to melt through the entire ice crust.\n\nUnlike true volcanic worlds where molten rock erupts, cryovolcanic eruptions involve melted volatiles — water, ammonia, methane, and other ices that behave like magma at cryogenic temperatures. The core, heated by gravitational tidal flexing from a nearby gas giant or large moon, or by radioactive decay, generates enough warmth to partially melt subsurface ice layers. This melted material builds up as vapor and pressure beneath the thick frozen crust until the stress fractures the ice from below.\n\nThe resulting eruptions are geysers of superheated vapor, slush, and frozen particulates blasting through kilometers of ice. These vapor eruptions can be powerful enough to reach escape velocity — launching plumes of vapor and ice particles directly into space, visible from orbit.\n\nCryovolcanic worlds are sometime exploited for their volatiles but most are left on their own."
      },
      "frozen-planet": {
        "text": "Frozen planets are worlds that orbit so far from their star that they do not receive enough energy to maintain a relatively warm global temperature.\n\nTheir surfaces take different forms depending on what the planet was before it froze. When the planet lacked a thick enough atmosphere, the crust is simply frozen rock: a rigid, brittle shell of stone and ice-hardened minerals, scarred by impact craters and cracked by thermal contraction. There is little to distinguish the surface from a barren world except the temperature — cold enough to shatter unprotected metal and to freeze most fluids solid.\n\nWhen the planet once had a substantial atmosphere, the surface is often covered by the frozen remains of that atmosphere — layers of solidified gases, nitrogen ice, carbon dioxide ice, methane frost, and other volatiles that once floated freely as gas. These frozen atmospheric deposits are sometimes exploited for volatile materials: a valuable and accessible source of compounds that are otherwise energy-intensive to produce. Mining operations on such worlds are essentially glacier-mining — cutting blocks of frozen gas and transporting them to orbital refineries for processing.\n\nSome frozen planets are hidden water worlds. Beneath kilometers of solid ice crust, the combination of internal geothermal heat and tidal flexing can maintain a liquid water ocean — dark, cold, but unfrozen — sealed away from the void of space by an insulating shell of ice that can be dozens of kilometers thick. These subsurface oceans can be vast, containing more liquid water than some temperate worlds. Reaching them requires deep-ice drilling through the crust, and the conditions within — high pressure, near-freezing temperatures, and total darkness — make exploration difficult but not impossible for a civilization with the right technology."

      "toxic-planet": {
        "text": "Toxic planets are Venus-like worlds with dense, crushing atmospheres. They orbit close enough to their star that the atmosphere never freezes and rains back down — instead it remains a thick, superheated blanket of gases. The atmosphere is most often dominated by CO2, along with a multitude of other toxic and acidic gases: sulfuric acid, hydrogen sulfide, hydrofluoric acid, chlorine, and others. Surface conditions are extreme — temperatures hot enough to melt lead, pressures dozens of times that of a standard atmosphere, and corrosive atmospheres that dissolve unshielded equipment within hours.\n\nMost toxic planets are ignored entirely, offering nothing worth the enormous cost and risk of operating in such an environment. However, some are exploited when a particular layer of the atmosphere becomes dense and rich enough in a single valuable element or compound to justify the investment.\n\nThe most common extraction method is an orbital station that dispatches specialized atmospheric craft. This approach is expensive but relatively reliable and keeps personnel in orbit away from the worst conditions.\n\nFor the most technologically advanced civilizations, a floating platform — maintained aloft by constant thruster fire or antigravitic engines — can be stationed directly within one of the more 'livable' atmospheric layers, where temperature, pressure, and corrosion are marginally tolerable for the species involved. These platforms allow continuous on-site extraction and processing, but require constant maintenance and enormous energy expenditure.\n\nThe planetary crust itself is almost always completely ignored. The combination of extreme heat, corrosive gases under high pressure, and the sheer difficulty of reaching the surface through the thick atmosphere makes ground-level operations wildly impractical. What really lies below remains largely a mystery — most surveys content themselves with radio scans and LIDAR."

      "volcanic-planet": {
        "text": "A rocky planet whose surface is partially or fully molten. This can result from several causes: orbiting close enough to its star that the surface temperature keeps the crust fused; having just finished its formation and still retaining the heat of accretion; a recent impact with another celestial body — an asteroid, a rogue moon, or even a small planet — that liquefied the crust in a cataclysmic collision; or a core unusually rich in transplutonic elements whose radioactive decay generates enough heat to keep the planet partially melted from within. In every case except the first (solar proximity), given a few hundred million years the planet will eventually cool down and become a barren world.\n\nThe surface of a volcanic planet is a hellscape of rivers of molten rock, lakes of magma, and constant volcanic eruptions. The ground itself radiates heat intense enough to warp or melt unshielded metal. Tectonic activity is violent and continuous — the crust is thin, fractured, and constantly reshaped by upwellings of magma from below. Volcanic plumes rise kilometers into the atmosphere, carrying ash, sulfur compounds, and vaporized metals. Where the crust is thicker, it buckles and cracks under the pressure from below, creating vast rift valleys that glow orange with exposed magma vents. The air, where any atmosphere exists, is thick with sulfurous fumes, superheated steam, and aerosolized minerals — toxic and corrosive to most life and equipment.\n\nDespite — or rather because of — these conditions, volcanic planets are prime targets for heavy and mineral industry. The constant volcanic activity acts as a natural smelting furnace: it brings plumes of mineral-rich lava and magma to the surface from deep within the mantle, concentrating rare and valuable elements that would otherwise remain inaccessible. Volcanic worlds are valuable for both ordinary ore extraction and transplutonic mining: the constant magma upwelling brings up common industrial metals — iron, copper, titanium, tungsten — alongside rarer veins. Transplutonic-rich volcanic worlds in particular can offer concentrations of ultra-heavy metals and exotic isotopes found almost nowhere else. The intense subsurface heat also provides virtually unlimited geothermal power — boreholes into the crust can tap steam and thermal energy on a scale that dwarfs any conventional power source.\n\nExploitation requires the most hardened infrastructure imaginable. Surface installations must be built with refractory materials, heat shielding, and active cooling systems just to survive. Many operations are fully automated or remotely operated, with drones and robotic harvesters collecting cooled lava flows for processing. More daring operations establish platforms anchored to the thickest available crust, or even floating platforms held aloft above the worst zones by thrusters — similar to those used on toxic worlds, but designed for heat rather than corrosion. Personnel, when present at all, live in pressurized, climate-controlled habitats and rotate frequently to avoid the cumulative stress of the environment.\n\nThe risk is matched only by the reward: a single rich volcanic planet can supply an entire industrial sector with rare metals, isotopes, and energy for decades. But the margin between a profitable operation and a catastrophic loss — a crust breach, a magma surge, an eruption swallowing an entire installation — is razor-thin."

      "alpine-planet": {
        "text": "Alpine worlds are a type of temperate planet whose landmasses are dominated by mountains and hills. These towering ranges shape habitable zones by blocking humid winds and creating distinct microclimates on their slopes and in the valleys between them.\n\nAltitude governs everything — temperature, vegetation, and habitability shift dramatically as one climbs from warm lowland valleys to frozen peaks, creating stacked ecological zones on a single mountainside. A typical alpine world might feature lush river valleys at its base, dense forests on the lower slopes, hardy shrublands and alpine meadows at middle elevations, and bare rock plus permanent snow and ice at the summits. The windward side of a range may be wet and forested while the leeward side sits in a rain shadow — dry, rocky, and sparse.\n\nThe terrain makes surface travel difficult and infrastructure expensive. Settlements tend to cluster in valley floors and on natural plateaus, connected by mountain passes that may be impassable for much of the year. Mining is the most common industry — the tectonic activity that builds the mountains also pushes mineral-rich veins to accessible depths — but the cost of transport and the harshness of high-altitude operations limit exploitation to the richest deposits.\\n\\nDespite the challenges, alpine worlds support surprising biodiversity. The isolation created by rugged terrain fragments populations into distinct pockets, encouraging speciation and endemic species. Each valley may hold unique flora and fauna found nowhere else on the planet, making alpine worlds prized by biologists and surveyors — though the same remoteness that protects biodiversity also makes cataloguing it a slow and arduous endeavor."
      },
      "marsh-planet": {
        "text": "Marsh planets are dominated by lowlands where water stalls and accumulates, sitting on the colder side of the habitable planet spectrum. This richness sometimes convinces settlers to develop small towns in the driest patches of the global swamp — raised ground, natural levees, or artificial mounds built up over generations — where they practice agriculture and harvest the abundant organic resources the wetland provides."

      "raw-ressources": {
        "text": "Raw ressources is the wide term for all basic resources as they are extracted from the environment — the unrefined, unprocessed materials that form the backbone of all economy. Before any manufacturing, refining, or synthesis, every product begins as a raw resource harvested from a planet, moon, asteroid, or gas giant.\n\nThe main categories of raw ressources are:\n\n- Organics — bulk complex carbon-based molecules and derivatives: hydrocarbons, wood, coal, plastics, fuels, solvents, polymers, biotech\n- Ore — ferrous and common non-ferrous metallic ores, up to and excluding plutonium\n- Transplutonic ore — unprocessed heavy elements: rare earths, actinides, exotic minerals\n- Exotics — materials that defy conventional physics\n- Volatiles — gaseous elements and compounds: hydrogen, helium, nitrogen, noble gases\n- Food — vegetal, fungal, and animal products vital for carbon-based life"
      },
      "organics": {
        "text": "Bulk complex carbon-based molecules and derivatives thereof with applications in plastics, fuels, solvents, polymers, biotech, and a vast array of other necessities. Hydrocarbons make up the majority — methane, petroleum, natural gases, and all their derivatives — but wood, coal, and other carbon-based biological materials technically fit in too. Organics are among the most versatile raw resources: they serve as fuel, feedstock for chemical industries, building materials, and the foundation for synthesizing more complex compounds."
      },
      "ore": {
        "text": "Includes ores of both ferrous and common non-ferrous metals. Must be refined to be of use to industry. Ore is the wide term for any metallic ore that contains elements up to and excluding plutonium on the periodic table — everything from common iron, copper, and aluminum to precious metals like gold, silver, and platinum, as well as industrial metals like titanium, tungsten, and chromium. Ore is the backbone of conventional industry: construction, manufacturing, electronics, and infrastructure all depend on the steady supply and refining of these metals."
      },
      "transplutonic-ore": {
        "text": "Unprocessed heavy elements that may include rare earths, actinides, and more exotic minerals essential to advanced industrial and research applications. Transplutonic ore contains elements past and including plutonium on the periodic table — americium, curium, berkelium, californium, and beyond. These elements are among the rarest and most valuable in the universe, found almost exclusively in volcanic planets where radioactive decay in the core keeps the planet partially melted, or in the debris of rare celestial events like supernovae and neutron star collisions."
      },
      "exotics": {
        "text": "Exotics is the wide term for any material that does not fit the laws of physics as they were understood by 21st-century science. These are substances that defy conventional understanding — matter with negative mass, stable superheavy elements that should not exist, materials that allow the manipulation of gravity, space-time, or fundamental forces in ways classical physics cannot explain. "

      "volatiles": {
        "text": "Volatiles is the wide term for all gaseous elements and compounds that do not fit in the organics or ore categories — primarily hydrogen, helium, nitrogen, oxygen, argon, neon, and other noble or elemental gases, as well as simple non-organic gaseous compounds. Volatiles are essential across countless industries: hydrogen and helium for fusion power and lighter-than-air craft, nitrogen and oxygen for atmosphere synthesis and life support, noble gases for lighting, shielding, and industrial processes. They are most commonly harvested from gas giants, frozen planets with solidified atmospheric deposits, and the atmospheres of toxic worlds."

      "food": {

On worlds where agriculture is impossible — volcanic, toxic, frozen, barren, or gas giant moons — food must be imported or produced in controlled environments at significant cost, making it a critical supply chain concern for any colony, outpost, or expedition operating far from habitable worlds."

      "metals": {
        "text": "Refined forms of both ferrous and common non-ferrous metals used in most construction and goods production. Once raw ore is mined, it is smelted, purified, and alloyed into workable metals — iron into steel, bauxite into aluminum, copper refined for electronics, titanium forged for aerospace structures. Metals are the intermediate building blocks of all manufacturing: they are used by other industries to make more complex goods, from spacecraft hulls and machinery components to electronics, construction materials, and consumer products. Without a steady supply of refined metals, no industrial economy can function."

While not strategically critical like fuel or armaments, domestic goods drive the daily economy of any civilization — colonies need them for comfort and productivity, citizens demand them for quality of life, and trade in domestic goods forms the commercial backbone of most settled worlds."

Luxury goods are far less demanded than domestic goods in volume but command vastly higher prices, making them a lucrative niche trade for merchants willing to cater to the elite. On frontier worlds where basic supplies are scarce, the presence of luxury goods is a stark reminder of wealth inequality — a bottle of aged wine can cost more than a miner's annual wage."

      "machineries": {

      "FTL": {
        "text": "FTL is the familiar term for faster than light. FTL drives are the broad designation for all technological means of achieving faster-than-light travel. The known FTL methods include warp drives, hyperlane drives, wormhole stations, and the exotic inertia drives found only in Forerunner ships. Each method differs in speed, freedom, infrastructure requirements, and energy cost, but all serve the same fundamental purpose: moving ships across interstellar distances."

      "warp-drive": {
        "text": "Warp drives are engines that allow FTL travel by warping the space around the ship to create a bubble of spacetime. By moving the bubble faster than light, the ship inside is carried along without ever locally exceeding the speed of light — the ship never moves faster than light within its own bubble, but the bubble itself can travel at superluminal speeds relative to the rest of the universe.\n\nThe warp scale works as a multiplier of the speed of light: warp 1 equals light speed, warp 2 equals light speed squared, warp 3 equals light speed cubed, and so on. Technically a warp drive can reach infinite speed, but the energy cost ramps up so dramatically that most engines only go as fast as warp 3.\n\nWarp drive is the freest FTL method: any ship equipped with one can point itself in any direction and engage its drive, as long as it has fuel. No pre-existing infrastructure, no fixed routes, no external assistance required — just fuel and a clear direction."
      },
      "wormhole-station": {
        "text": "Wormhole stations are hyper-tech-level infrastructure using exotic materials and machines to pierce a tunnel through realspace to another point, allowing instant translation between two locations. They have a limited range of roughly 20 light years, so civilizations with the resources often construct highways of wormhole stations — chains linking system to system — allowing ships to travel at a much faster rate than any other FTL system.\n\nEach station must follow a schedule, linking different systems during a given period before powering down, changing parameters, and opening a new wormhole to the next scheduled destination. This scheduling creates massive queues — often hundreds of thousands of kilometers long — of civilian traders and travelers waiting for their destination to be dialed in. The sheer density of ships assembled at these choke points makes piracy sadly unavoidable.\n\nMilitary forces often have dedicated wormhole stations and can requisition civilian ones to facilitate the rapid deployment of fleets, making wormhole infrastructure a strategic asset of the highest order — whoever controls the stations controls the flow of interstellar traffic."
      },
      "hyperlane drives": {
        "text": "Hyperlane drives are FTL engines that allow a ship to slip into a subspace dimension — corridors that link some star systems together. Faster than warp drives, most hyperlanes allow the equivalent of warp 5 speed, but travel is limited by the hyperlane network itself.\n\nHyperlanes are only reachable by infusing spacetime with energy at small weak points found in the outskirts of star systems, beyond the gravitational influence of the star. These entry points link only certain star systems together: some systems have multiple hyperlanes, others only one, and some have zero — completely isolated from the network.\n\nOnce inside a hyperlane, a ship cannot simply turn around. It must complete its translation, emerge at the other end, and wait for the engine to warm up before diving again to return. This makes hyperlane travel a commitment — there is no mid-course reversal.\n\nWhile not as much of a choke point as wormhole stations, hyperlanes can only be reached in certain zones of any given star system, creating a risk of ambush at both entry and exit points. Pirates and enemy fleets often lie in wait near hyperlane termini, where arriving ships are vulnerable and predictable."

      "inertia-drives": {

No conventional physics can explain this: the drive effectively decouples the vessel from inertial mass, allowing unlimited acceleration without the crew feeling any force. These drives are among the most coveted pieces of Forerunner technology — any civilization that could replicate them would gain an insurmountable advantage in both travel and combat, as a ship unbound by inertia can outmaneuver anything constrained by conventional physics."

        "text": "Light industries are the broad name for the production of consumer and luxury goods. Examples include electronics production, appliance manufacturing, furniture assembly, textile fabrication, craft goods, and the production of medicinal and recreational drugs. Light industries are less resource-intensive and less polluting than heavy industries, and their facilities can be established on most habitable worlds with a modest industrial base."

      "manufactorum": {
        "text": "Manufactorum is the name given to light industrial sectors that have developed so much that the sheer scale of production creates a qualitative change. When properly planned, every factory feeds into another — the output of one becoming the input of the next — reducing greatly the logistical element of production. Components, subassemblies, and finished goods flow between facilities with minimal transport overhead, creating a self-reinforcing industrial ecosystem where efficiency scales with size.\n\nA manufactorum is not just a cluster of factories but an integrated production network: raw materials enter at one end and finished consumer goods, luxury goods, electronics, pharmaceuticals, and all manner of light industrial products emerge at the other, having passed through dozens of specialized stages without ever leaving the complex. This level of integration requires enormous upfront planning and investment, but once established, a manufactorum can outproduce dozens of scattered independent factories at a fraction of the per-unit cost."

      "heavy-industries": {
        "text": "Heavy industries are all the industries that revolve primarily around metals and their transformation into products — from producing weapons of all sizes to ship hulls and components. Ships exceeding this size must be constructed in orbital works instead. Heavy industrial facilities are resource-intensive, polluting, and require significant infrastructure, making them impractical on all but the most industrially developed worlds."

      "orbital-works": {
        "text": "Orbital works are the next step after heavy industries. The absence of gravity means bigger structures, bigger assemblies, and bigger output, unconstrained by the launch limitations of planetary industry. Orbital works are the backbone of any serious spacefaring civilization — without them, no fleet of meaningful size can be built."

        "core_principles": "# NPC INTENT INSTRUCTIONS\n\nYou generate what NPCs do. The story generator writes the scene.\n\n## FORMAT\nEvery intent begins with one verb in brackets, then the action.\n\n[WORKING] Merrik keeps counting the coins and answers without looking up.\n\nThe verb is not narrated. It tells the story generator how this person\nis behaving so it can write them correctly.\n\n## THE TWELVE VERBS\n- WORKING — mid-task. The player is an interruption\n- ASKING — wants something they cannot get alone\n- TENDING — caring for, feeding, protecting, staying near someone\n- EASING — company with nothing to accomplish. Banter, teasing,\n  complaining, killing time, enjoying the moment\n- TESTING — competing, challenging, showing off, measuring themselves\n  against someone\n- PROBING — trying to find something out\n- GUARDING — holding back, withholding, covering, keeping something\n  out of reach\n- AVOIDING — wants distance, wants out, wants it over\n- STRIKING — straightforward attack. No angle needed\n- PRESSING — pushing for something against resistance\n- OFFERING — giving, trading, proposing, surrendering\n- OPPOSING — actively against the player. Out of combat only\n\nPick the verb first. Then write the move.\n\nNot every scene is a transaction. When nothing is at stake and the\npeople present like each other, EASING is the correct verb and often\nthe only one.\n\n## ABILITIES ARE HOW, NOT WHAT\nAn NPC's abilities are the way they execute a verb, not a verb of their\nown. Growing to twice someone's height and lifting them off the ground\nis STRIKING. Dropping your own weight to nothing and landing behind\nsomeone is AVOIDING.\n\nRead the character's abilities and use them. A fighter who never uses\nwhat she has is written wrong.\n\n## WHAT AN INTENT IS\nOne concrete thing an NPC does because of what they want.\n\n- A target: who or what it is aimed at\n- A mechanism: what they use\n- A change: what is different afterward\n\nIf you cannot name all three, it is not an intent.\n\n## THE MECHANISM COMES FROM THE WORLD\nAn NPC uses what is actually there: the ground, objects in reach, who\nelse is present, what is owed, what is known, who is watching, how much\ntime there is, what they are afraid of losing.\n\nAn intent that could happen in an empty white room is a weak intent.\n\n## NO DIALOGUE\nNever write what an NPC says. Never write quoted speech. Write the move.\n\"Merrik sets a price that assumes they are desperate\" is an intent.\nAnything containing his words is not.\n\n## PRINCIPLES\n- NPCs act on their own goals.         "when_to_generate": "## WHEN TO GENERATE INTENTS\n\n### In Combat\nAll NPCs actively fighting. Count by tier:\n- trivial/weak: 1\n- average: 1-2\n- strong: 2\n- elite/boss/mythic: 2-3\n\nMultiple intents for one NPC should not share a verb.\n\n### Out of Combat\nSTRICT LIMIT: at most 1-2 NPCs.         "what_is_not_action": "## WHAT IS NOT AN INTENT\n\n### The \"What Changes?\" Test\nIf this resolves, what is different afterward? If the answer is nothing,\nit is not an intent.\n\n### Not intents\n- Internal states: considers, evaluates, weighs, suspects, worries\n- Meaningful looks: eyes gleam, fixes them with a stare, watches closely\n- Posing: how someone stands, holds themselves, or carries a weapon\n- Reactions: flinches, stiffens, laughs, goes quiet\n- Speech: anything that is a line of dialogue rather than a move\n- Atmosphere or environmental pressure\n- Suspicion with nothing done about it\n\n### The Rule\nAn NPC standing there thinking gets no intent. The story generator\nhandles ambient behavior without you.",
        "description_economy": "## HOW EACH VERB MOVES\n\n**WORKING** — continues the task. Answers while doing something else,\ndefers, sets the interruption aside, finishes first. Usually no intent.\n\n**ASKING** — asks directly. Shows what they have already tried, brings\nthe broken thing, names what it would cost them. No angle. People who\nneed help ask for help.\n\n**TENDING** — gives, feeds, covers, stays near, takes the harder share.\nOften does it so it will not be noticed.\n\n**EASING** — company with no task attached. Teases, complains, tells the\nstory again, needles someone they like, eats, sits down, gets bored,\nbrings up something unrelated, enjoys the moment they are in. Also where\nan NPC opens up about themselves unprompted. Nothing is being\naccomplished, and that is the point.\n\n**TESTING** — challenges, competes, shows off, sizes someone up, pushes\nto see what they can do, makes a contest of something that did not need\nto be one. Not seeking information — seeking the measure of someone.\n\n**PROBING** — asks a question with a second purpose, tests a claim,\noffers something to see the response, brings up a name and watches.\n\n**GUARDING** — withholds, answers less than was asked, moves the thing\nout of reach, puts a person or object between, keeps a door closed.\n\n**AVOIDING** — leaves, defers, makes the thing difficult instead of\nrefusing, sends someone else, prices it out of reach, goes quiet.\n\n**STRIKING** — attacks. Commits to a strike, closes distance, presses\nthe advantage, uses the ability the character actually has. No angle, no\nleverage, no environment required. Sometimes the right move is to hit\nsomeone.\n\nSTRIKING is the one verb exempt from the mechanism requirement. A target\nand an effect are enough. Most attacks would work in an empty room, and\nthat is what an attack is.\n\nDo not dress up a plain attack as a tactic. If a fighter is simply\nhitting someone, tag it STRIKING and write the blow.\n\n**PRESSING** — closes the alternative, attaches a condition, names a\nprice, gets a position stated in front of others, makes refusal costly.\n\n**OFFERING** — proposes, trades, gives something up, sets terms,\nsurrenders, puts the thing on the table.\n\n**OPPOSING** — the full toolkit: deny the option, exploit the weakness,\nchange the ground, add or remove a witness, commit them, raise the cost,\nredirect, take the thing. Out of combat only, and only when opposition\nalready exists.\n\n### Competence\nRead personality, skills, and role. The same verb produces different\nmoves from different people.\n\nCapable characters work indirectly — arranging things so the outcome is\noffered rather than demanded.\n\nWeak or frightened characters use a narrow range: put a person or object\nbetween themselves and the threat, move toward other people rather than\naway from danger, refuse by making the thing difficult, give the thing\nup early to end the pressure, lie and then hold the lie.\n\nDo not make every NPC clever. A scene where everyone manoeuvres well is\nas false as one where nobody does.\n\n### Scale\nMatch the move to how much this moment matters to this NPC. Most moves\nare small. A large one needs a reason already in the scene.\n\n### Cut\n- Tone, gestures, expressions, poses\n- Atmospheric description\n- Anything the story generator will write anyway",

Si procede, vincula su objeto con ItemGenerationAndUsage.\n\nEJES (rutas distintas que coexisten):\n- EVOLUCIÓN: progresión natural del mismo núcleo (más alcance, mismo origen).\n- VARIANTE: adaptación del mismo núcleo a otro uso sin cambiar su identidad (misma raíz, otra rama).\n- MUTACIÓN: reescritura que lo aleja de su origen (regla o riesgo nuevo, forma distinta, a veces inestable).\nRareza y riesgo suben con la distancia a lo humano.\n\nESCALAS:\n- Humano/cyberpunk local: implantes, artesanía, trato, supervivencia 2184.\n- Técnica-ciencia 2184: ingeniería, protocolos, pilotaje, análisis dimensional.\n- MÁS GRANDE (transhumano/dimensional/no-humano): capacidades que criatura o Cicatriz enseñan y exceden lo humano (física de entidad, lógica de portal, crecimiento biometálico), siempre con coste, riesgo y rareza; nunca gratis.\n\n## Balance\nRestricciones de origen, función, material, energía, requisitos.
